sources.news_title: Partial solar eclipse, Perseid meteors in New Hampshire skies this week
sources.text:
Partial solar eclipse, Perseid meteors in New Hampshire skies this week
Granite Staters can look to the skies this week to catch a partial solar eclipse and a spectacular meteor shower.
Anyone who has eclipse glasses handy can see a bite being taken out of the sun on Wednesday afternoon.
People in parts of Europe will be able to see a total solar eclipse, but in New Hampshire, only about 16-20% of the sun will be covered by the passing moon.
That means there won't be any real noticeable difference in the sunlight Wednesday unless you use special glasses or another method, such as a pinhole projector, to see the partial eclipse.
The partial eclipse will start just before 1 p.m. in New Hampshire and reach its maximum point at 1:50 p.m. to 1:54 p.m., depending on your location. It ends at about 2:45 p.m.
Because the eclipse is only partial, it will remain unsafe to look at the sun without protection. Many people still have eclipse glasses from the last two total eclipses that crossed the United States in recent years. It's important to check those glasses for any damage before using them. If they have any tears, scratches or folds in the lenses, they shouldn't be used.
>> Meteorologist Jacqueline Thomas shows how to make a pinhole projector
PERSEID METEOR SHOWER
The Perseid meteor shower peaks overnight Wednesday into Thursday, and it should be a great night of viewing if the skies remain clear.
The peak coincides with a new moon, which earlier eclipsed the sun. That means there will be no moonlight to interfere with the meteor shower.
For best viewing, find an open, dark location away from city lights. Meteors can be seen across the sky, and there should be dozens of meteors an hour.
Clouds could be an issue. Some clouds are expected at around 11 p.m., with partly cloudy skies at around 2 a.m. Skies will be clearer toward dawn.
Perseid meteors can be seen in the days before and after the peak, as well.

sources.news_title: Hundreds of meteors expected to light up the sky during Perseids peak
sources.text:
Hundreds of meteors expected to light up the sky during Perseids peak
The annual meteor shower peaks Wednesday
The annual meteor shower peaks Wednesday
The peak of the annual Perseid meteor shower is expected to send hundreds of visible shooting stars across the sky this Wednesday night.
The Perseids come around every summer as a result of a dust cloud flying off comet Swift-Tuttle. This year the shower began July 17 and will continue until Aug 23. But the pairing of the highest concentration of passing meteors on Aug 12 with a new moon may provide some of the best conditions to see the shooting stars.
According to NASA the shower will start to be visible after 10 p.m. in the northeast part of the sky, originating from the Perseus constellation, the Perseids’ namesake. Every hour, 50-100 meteors are expected to pass through the sky until the early morning of Aug 13.
Because of the new moon on Wednesday, the night sky should be darker than normal, helping to make the meteors clearer and more vibrant during the peak of the shower.
However, wildfire smoke rolling in from the western side of the country and Canada may blot out visibility to the dimmer meteors, according to StormTeam 5 meteorologist AJ Bernett. The possibility of cloudy skies might also affect clarity, so keep an eye on the weather as we approach the shower’s peak.
In any case, experts recommend heading away from city lights as light pollution makes it harder to see stars and passing meteors.
Allowing your eyes to adjust to the darkness before watching the showers begin will also help with visibility, NASA said. Turn off all lights, including phone screens, at least 30 minutes before stargazing.
If you aren't able to catch the Perseid shower in person this year, don't worry. The shooting stars are visible from the northern hemisphere every year.

sources.news_title: How and When to View the Perseid Meteor Shower This Week
sources.text:
In addition to a historic total solar eclipse, August also features one of the most spectacular meteor showers of the year. On the night of August 12 and into the early morning of August 13, astronomy enthusiasts in the northern hemisphere and parts of the southern hemisphere will be able to admire the Perseids during a particularly favorable viewing window.
Occasionally, Earth passes through the trails of particles left behind by some comets as they travel through the solar system. When these tiny fragments enter Earth’s atmosphere, friction with the air heats them until they burn up. From below, it looks as though the sky is filled with bright flashes streaking across the heavens at high speed. These are meteor showers. There are several throughout the year, and the one in August is called the Perseids.
Although a meteor shower is one of the few astronomical phenomena that can be observed with the naked eye, it is not always easy to track. To enjoy it to the fullest, it’s a good idea to follow some basic recommendations for stargazing.
This Year’s Perseids Are Especially Visible
Traditionally, the Perseids reach a rate of up to 100 meteors per hour during their peak activity—at least, under ideal viewing conditions. This makes them one of the three most intense meteor showers of the year, along with the Geminids in December and the Quadrantids in January.
In 2026, the viewing conditions are particularly favorable. The peak of activity, expected on the night of August 12–13, will coincide with the new moon phase. This means that virtually none of the moon’s illuminated side will be visible from Earth, so there will be no moonlight to interfere with meteor viewing. In other words, the sky will be much darker than usual.
What’s the Best Way to View the Perseids?
The main advice from NASA and the European Space Agency (ESA) for enjoying a meteor shower is to get away from light pollution. Ideally, head out of the city and find a spot with dark skies, as well as a horizon that’s as unobstructed as possible to ensure a wide field of view.
Keep in mind that it takes the human eyes 20 to 30 minutes to fully adjust to the dark. Once that time has passed, it will be easier to spot faint meteors. While observing, it’s also advisable to avoid using your cell phone or other bright screens, as they reduce your eyes’ sensitivity.
Another important tip is to avoid using telescopes and binoculars. Although they might seem useful, NASA explains that these instruments narrow your field of view, whereas meteors can appear anywhere in the sky. It’s best to observe with the naked eye.
Although the Perseids get their name because they appear to radiate from the constellation Perseus, it is not necessary to look toward it. Both NASA and the ESA point out that meteors can streak across any part of the sky. Ideally, lie down or use a reclining chair to observe a wide portion of the sky, preferably after midnight, when the meteor shower’s radiant reaches a higher point above the horizon and the frequency of visible meteors increases.
Finally, the agencies remind us that patience is also part of the experience. Meteors do not appear at a steady rate. Several minutes may pass without any activity, and then suddenly, several may be seen in quick succession. Staying under a dark sky for at least an hour offers the best chance of enjoying the show.
This story originally appeared on WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.

sources.news_title: Date Perseid meteor shower will reach its peak this week - and the best time frame to look for the Perseids
sources.text:
Date Perseid meteor shower will reach its peak this week - and the best time frame to look for the Perseids
You could see up to 100 meteors per hour during the Perseid meteor shower.
The solar eclipse is not the only astronomical event happening this week. You might also be able to catch the Perseid meteor shower as it reaches its peak.
Here’s all you need to know about the Perseid meteor shower, including the best time to look for the Perseids.
The Perseid meteor shower explained
Royal Museums Greenwich explains that as comets get close to the Sun, they heat up and pieces break off. If the debris gets in the Earth’s path around the Sun, it can slam into our atmosphere at speeds of between seven to 45 miles per second. The average speed for a Perseid meteor is 36 miles per second.
How to see the Perseid meteor shower
You should try to reduce the amount of light pollution. You could do this by heading out to the countryside, a nearby park or turning away from street lights. Give your eyes at least 15 minutes to adjust to the dark.
Try to get into a position where you can see lots of sky as meteors can appear in any part of the sky. Find an area with a clear view of the horizon away from trees and buildings. Binoculars and telescopes are not necessary as they will restrict the size of the sky that will be visible to you.
What direction to look for the Perseid meteor shower
The meteors will seem to originate from the constellation of Perseus. Royal Museums Greenwich says you can use a stargazing app to find the exact location to look.
When the Perseid meteor shower will peak
In 2026, the Perseid meteor shower is active between 17 July and 24 August. The number of meteors will increase every night until it reaches the peak, which is in the early morning hours between midnight and dawn on 12 and 13 August this year.
What is the best time to look for the Perseid meteor shower
According to Royal Museums Greenwich, observers in the UK should be able to see some meteors as soon as the Sun sets.
In 2026, the peak of the Perseid meteor shower fortunately occurs during new Moon, so conditions are ideal for seeing the peak. The best time to see the Perseids is between midnight and 5.30am. It is always ideal to try to spot meteors when the Moon is below the horizon or when it is in its crescent phase, otherwise it acts as natural light pollution.

sources.news_title: How to have the best chance of seeing the Perseid meteor shower
sources.text:
How to have the best chance of seeing the Perseid meteor shower in Maine
The Perseid meteor shower is expected to be spectacular this year, peaking Wednesday night into early Thursday morning. Although the streaks of light will be visible from many places, specific times and locations will help increase your chances of seeing the greatest number of meteors possible.
These meteors will specifically be debris from Comet Swift-Tuttle, which passes by our sun every 133 years. The leftover particles from the comet passing by will hit Earth's atmosphere and burn up in the sky. The Perseid meteor shower could potentially create fireballs and colorful streaks of light as debris hits the atmosphere, so you might be lucky enough to catch a red, green, or even blue streak across the sky. Even if you don’t get to see the color streaks, yellow meteors will be noticeable.
The number of meteors per hour changes every year when the Perseid meteor shower occurs, but during the peak this year, people can expect 50 to 100 meteors in ideal conditions.
As of Tuesday morning, cloud cover for the peak activity of the meteor shower is looking partly cloudy. Scattered showers and thunderstorms are possible inland and Midcoast overnight Wednesday into Thursday morning. Southern Maine could remain dry, but that doesn’t rule out nuisance cloud cover. To avoid the chances for rain clouds, some meteors will also be visible throughout the week, but the new moon is what keeps people hopeful about Wednesday night's visibility.
To have the best chance of seeing the Perseid meteor shower, find a time between midnight on Wednesday and sunrise on Thursday for the best visibility. A few meteors may be visible around 10 p.m. Wednesday if you want to watch them before bed, but meteor counts are going to climb after midnight and into the early morning. Technically, meteors can be found any time between mid-July and late August, so a few meteors will be visible this week.
Get away from cities and light pollution so that the night sky is extra dark for viewing. We will have a new moon Wednesday night during the peak as well, so skies won’t be illuminated by the moon. To keep yourself comfortable, bring warm layers and blankets, because temperatures can still be cold overnight in the summer months. Also, a can of bug spray will be helpful if you want to watch outside. Arrive early and make sure to turn phones and flashlights off about 30 minutes before you want to see the meteors so that your eyes have time to adjust to the dark.
The meteors will appear to be coming from a single point in the sky, also known as the radiant. Although the meteors will seem to originate from the Perseus constellation in the northeast sky, streaks of light will be visible anywhere in the sky, so you don’t need to look at a single point the whole entire night.

sources.news_title: Perseid meteor shower peaks Wednesday night: Where and how to view the cosmic display
sources.text:
The Perseid meteor shower is considered one of the best of the year, and it peaks Wednesday night.
It’s called the Perseid meteor shower because the meteors radiate from the constellation Perseus, which rises in the northeastern sky late in the evening – around 11 p.m. Perseus will make an arch through the northern sky overnight, so best viewing will be after midnight to sunrise on Thursday, when Perseus is high in the northern sky.
The meteors you’ll see are actually dust debris from the comet Swift-Tuttle – tiny grains or pebbles – that enter the earth’s atmosphere as the earth makes its annual pass through the comet’s debris field. It takes Swift-Tuttle 133 years to orbit the sun, and it last made its close pass through our solar system in 1992.
Watch NBC 4 free wherever you are
The comet’s debris enters the atmosphere at an incredible speed, about 37 miles per second. It’s so fast that the friction between the two causes the grains and the air they’re slicing through to heat up to about 3,000 degrees Fahrenheit – hot enough to produce the light that we see as a meteor.
The best way to view the Perseids is away from any light pollution. That means, get out of the city to a sparsely populated location. Once you’ve found a dark spot, look north toward Perseus and you could see up to 100 meteors per hour.
Star-gazers have a couple of things working in their favor during this year’s Perseids. First, the meteor shower’s peak falls on a new moon, which means there won’t be any moonlight to pollute the sky. Second, the forecast is for partly to mostly clear skies across the tri-state area, which means clouds shouldn’t be a big problem.
Also working in our favor is the time of year: summer. Low temperatures will be quite comfortable for viewing during the overnight period Wednesday night.
If you’re not able to catch the meteor shower Wednesday night, you’ll have other opportunities. The Perseids are actually visible all the way through Aug. 23. They’ll just be less active each night past the peak on August 12-13.

sources.news_title: Here's what you need to know about the Perseid meteor shower
This Week's Perseid Meteor Shower Could Be the Best Stargazing Event in Years
sources.text:
There are few sights that are as awe-inspiring as a sky suddenly alive with shooting stars. During the annual Perseid meteor shower, which occurs in August each year, bright streaks of white, amber, and the occasional emerald flash between familiar constellations, briefly illuminating the darkness before dissolving back into a sky so crowded with stars it hardly seems real. It's one of nature's most mesmerizing performances—and all you have to do is look up.
Under ideal dark sky conditions, observers can expect to see anywhere from 50 to 100 meteors an hour during the peak, with activity building after midnight and continuing until dawn. These so-called shooting stars are actually tiny fragments of ancient comet dust—many no larger than grains of sand—slamming into Earth's atmosphere at roughly 37 miles per second. The result? A steady parade of swift meteors, many leaving glowing trains behind them, punctuated by the occasional dazzling fireball that burns brighter than the stars themselves.
The Perseid meteor shower is widely regarded as the Northern Hemisphere's premier shooting star display—but this year, the timing just might be cosmic. This week, the shower's peak will almost perfectly align with the new moon, promising some of the best viewing conditions in years. Here's everything you need to know.
When is the 2026 Perseid meteor shower?
While the Perseid meteor shower is active from mid-July through late August, it will peak on the night of August 12 through the early morning hours of August 13, when Earth plows through the densest stream of debris left behind by Comet Swift-Tuttle. This year, that peak coincides almost perfectly with a new moon, leaving skies virtually free of moonlight and allowing even faint meteors to shine.
If you can't get away for Wednesday's show, this weekend will still offer favorable viewing conditions under the faint light of the crescent moon. That means you can still transform the experience into a last-minute summer road trip, national park day trip, or countryside escape for an unforgettable evening under the stars.
Where can I see the Perseids 2026?
Artificial light remains the single greatest obstacle to seeing the Perseids at their best, as light pollution washes out fainter meteors and dims the Milky Way overhead. But if you leave city lights behind, the night changes dramatically. Suddenly, constellations will sharpen into view, and meteors appear far more frequently. Basically, the darker your surroundings, the richer the experience becomes.
Across the Northern Hemisphere, travelers are spoiled for choice: In the United States, some of the country's most celebrated dark skies can be found at Bryce Canyon National Park in Utah, Big Bend National Park in Texas, Cherry Springs State Park in Pennsylvania, and Headlands International Dark Sky Park in Michigan.
In Canada, one of the best places to see the Perseids will be from Jasper National Park in Alberta. Meanwhile, Europe is home to internationally recognized dark-sky landscapes, including Galloway Forest Park in Scotland, Bannau Brycheiniog (Brecon Beacons) National Park in Wales, and Portugal's Alqueva Dark Sky Reserve. Together with hundreds of other accredited parks, reserves and communities recognized by DarkSky International, these destinations preserve the natural darkness that allows the Perseids to truly shine.
Where to stay
Where to book in the US:
- For an iconic inn upstate, New York: Whiteface Lodge
- For bucket-lust stargazing in Utah's Bryce Canyon: Clear Sky Resorts
- For an adventurous rental in Antelope, Oregon: StrawFork Cabin
- For a surreal casitas near Big Bend, West Texas: Willow House
- For a timeless and refined resort near Cape Lookout National Seashore: Beaufort Hotel NC
- For a stargazing New Mexico cabin with a hot tub: Behr Art #1
- For a stars-inspired group trip near Cherry Springs: Pennsylvania dream house rental
Where to book outside of the US:
- For a charming Alberta hub away from light pollution: Forest Park Hotel
- For a panoramic stay on Cardiff Bay: Voco St. David's Cardiff by IHG
- For a starry, secluded stay near Galloway Forest Park: The Pond Lodges Barstobrick
- For telescope views under Portugal's darkest skys: São Lourenco Do Barrocal
Viewing tips for the 2026 Perseid meteor shower
For travelers planning a dedicated meteor-shower getaway, flexibility is your greatest advantage. Build an extra night into your itinerary in case clouds roll in, and choose accommodations within easy reach of open viewpoints rather than brightly lit town centers. Wide horizons, dry air, and higher elevations often produce the clearest skies—while deserts, mountain ranges, and remote coastlines tend to boast the most dramatic viewing conditions.
Otherwise, the viewing itself is refreshingly uncomplicated. Leave the telescope behind; the naked eye offers the widest view of the sky, giving you the best chance of catching meteors streaking in every direction. Settle into a reclining chair or spread out a blanket, allow at least 20 minutes for your eyes to adjust to the darkness and resist the temptation to check your phone, whose bright screen quickly erases night vision. Layer up and dress more warmly than you think you'll need—even August nights can cool rapidly after sunset—and aim to stay out through the hours before dawn, when meteor activity is typically at its highest.

sources.news_title: Partial solar eclipse, Perseid meteor shower to grace Toronto’s skies this week. Here’s when to look up
sources.text:
A solar eclipse and the annual Perseid meteor shower are teaming up for a double feature of celestial events on Wednesday — and both will be visible from the Toronto area.
The solar eclipse, a phenomenon where the moon passes between the Earth and the sun and casts a shadow below, will be a daytime event. The eclipse will be partial in Canada, while the moon will fully block the sun in a total eclipse in parts of Western Europe.
The Perseid meteor shower will hit its peak between Wednesday night and the early hours of Thursday morning, when as many as 50 to 100 meteors per hour could be visible under ideal conditions, according to NASA.
Watching the partial solar eclipse in Toronto
The path of the total solar eclipse starts in the Arctic by Siberia, before passing the North Pole, the eastern side of Greenland, crossing Iceland and finishing in the northern half of Spain.
Canada lies outside the path of totality where the moon completely covers the sun, making the eclipse less dramatic. Instead viewers will see a partial eclipse that looks like the moon is taking a small bite out of the sun.
Toronto will see around eight per cent coverage. The partial eclipse begins in the afternoon at 12:55 p.m., reaching its peak at 1:40 p.m. and ending at 2:23 p.m.
Where will you be when the Sun puts on a show? ☀️
The August 12 partial solar eclipse will be visible across nearly all of Canada, but the timing and amount of the Sun covered will vary depending on your location.
📷: CSA pic.twitter.com/f5iR9O4Wcj
When looking at the sky during a solar eclipse, it’s crucial to wear special glasses to prevent eye damage, according to the Canadian Space Agency.
Glasses with filters designed for eclipse watching should meet the ISO 12312-2 international standard. Solar eclipses can also be viewed indirectly by constructing a small projector, like with a cardboard box.
Canada’s best views will be in northern areas like Iqaluit, where the moon is expected to cover around 61 per cent of the sun.
Unlike Wednesday’s partial event, large parts of the country were plunged into darkness on April 8, 2024, the last time Earth experienced a total solar eclipse.
The event drew thousands of spectators across southern Ontario, Quebec and the Maritimes, with the path of totality passing through Niagara Falls while just missing the Greater Toronto Area.
The next total solar eclipse that will be visible in Canada will occur on Aug. 22, 2044. That event will pass over the country’s western and northwestern provinces and territories, according to Ilana MacDonald, a spokesperson from the Dunlap Institute for Astronomy and Astrophysics at the University of Toronto.
“Total solar eclipses are very useful when it comes to studying the sun and even fundamental theories of space-time,” MacDonald wrote in an email to the Star.
A total solar eclipse was used to prove Einstein’s Theory of General Relativity, she added, noting that more recently, it’s mostly used to study the sun’s corona, which is only visible during a total solar eclipse.
Watching the Perseid meteor shower in Toronto
The Perseid meteor shower is an annual event where swift meteors shoot through the Earth’s atmosphere and leave behind streaks of light known as shooting stars.
The Perseids are debris from the comet 109P/Swift Tuttle, an icy ball that orbits around the sun every 133 years.
Walter Stoddard, senior scientist at the Ontario Science Centre, said late Wednesday evening until dawn is the best time to observe the meteors in the GTA, because the shower is expected to peak at 10:53 a.m. Thursday morning.
“The best time will be after midnight and before dawn — once the sky starts to brighten the show draws to a quick close,” Stoddard said, adding that as many as 100 meteors an hour could dash through the sky.
The Star, simplified

However, the meteors will be difficult to see in Toronto due to the artificial light produced in and around the city, so stargazers should plan to travel to darker skies.
“Find a dark viewing spot, away from the city lights and let your eyes adjust to the dark — this may take 20 minutes,” Stoddard said.
Skywatchers should know in advance where to find the constellation Perseus, the direction from which the meteors often come and dress for the weather during the night, Stoddard advised.
Clouds and possible rain loom in forecast
Cloudy skies could make it difficult to see the two phenomena in Toronto.
It’s expected to be sunny early Wednesday morning, followed by a mix of sun and cloud with 30 per cent chance of showers in the afternoon, when the eclipse is likely to be viewable, according to Environment Canada. The agency projects a daytime high of 24 C.
At night, when the meteor shower is expected to begin, the chances of showers will double to 60 per cent, with a nighttime low of 18 C, the weather agency says.
For those hoping to catch the meteor shower’s peak Thursday morning, the forecast calls for another mix of sun and clouds that day, along with a 40 per cent chance of showers and a high of 26 C.

sources.news_title: Will Perseid shooting stars be visible during the Aug. 12 total solar eclipse?
sources.text:
Will Perseid shooting stars be visible during the Aug. 12 total solar eclipse?
"If anyone does see one, they had better go play the lottery asap!"
A spectacular total solar eclipse will coincide with the peak of the Perseid meteor shower on Aug. 12-13. But will you be able to spot shooting stars in the false twilight of totality?
Perseids appear as Earth plows through the stream of debris shed by comet Swift-Tuttle. Up to 100 shooting stars may be seen each hour around its peak under ideal dark skies, as particles from the ancient comet collide with our atmosphere at speeds of 133,200 mph (214,365 km/h) to etch a fiery path through the summer night sky.
It's an unmissable highlight of the skywatching calendar, supercharged in 2026 by the spectacle of a total solar eclipse, which will plunge millions across Greenland, Iceland and Spain into the darkness of an eerie twilight, as the moon crosses the face of the sun.
Is it possible to see shooting stars during totality?
Yes. The most brilliant Perseid shooting stars can shine bright enough to be spotted in the brief twilight of totality. But it's all a question of timing.
"It would have to be a fireball that passed through the darkest portion of the sky," Robert Lunsford of the American Meteor Society told Space.com in an email. "The Perseids usually produce about one fireball per three hours at night. That's asking a lot for one of these bright meteors to appear during a 2-3 minute window. If anyone does see one, they had better go play the lottery asap!"
NASA Meteoroid Environments Office head Bill Cooke added his own word of caution, noting that the relatively bright sky during totality will likely hide all but the most brilliant Perseids from sight.
"Only Perseid fireballs will be visible," Cooke told Space.com in an email. "Given the brightness and duration of the eclipse, you might see one if you're extremely, extremely lucky. [The] most likely scenario is that you will see no meteors whatsoever."
The odds are definitely stacked against you. But you never know. A piece of comet Swift-Tuttle could've broken away at just the right time, at just the right point in its orbit to meet a fiery end in Earth's atmosphere, just as the sun slips from view. As for our advice? Keep your eyes locked firmly on the eclipse as it unfolds in the skies above you. There'll be plenty of time for hunting Perseids later.

sources.news_title: Solar Eclipse And Perseids Peak: What Time To Watch In U.S. And Canada
sources.text:
Topline
Skywatchers across the U.S. and Canada have two celestial events to catch within 24 hours. On Wednesday, Aug. 12, a partial solar eclipse will be visible across much of North America as a total solar eclipse sweeps across Greenland, Iceland and Spain. Then, after darkness falls, the annual Perseid meteor shower will peak beneath perfectly moonless skies. It brings together two of the celestial highlights of summer. Here’s exactly when to look up, where to get the best views and how to watch both safely.
Key Facts
A partial solar eclipse will be visible across Alaska, 26 U.S. states and every Canadian province and territory on Wednesday, Aug. 12.
The deepest eclipse in the contiguous U.S. will be seen from northern Maine, where the moon will cover up to 28% of the sun. Canada gets a much better show, with Nunavut seeing up to 61% obscuration and Newfoundland and Labrador more than 50%.
Anyone watching the eclipse must wear ISO 12312-2-certified eclipse glasses at all times. Binoculars, cameras and telescopes require securely fitted solar filters over the front of the optics.
Just hours after the eclipse ends, the annual Perseid meteor shower reaches its peak beneath almost perfectly moonless skies. Between about 2:00 and 4:00 a.m. local time on Thursday, Aug. 13, observers under dark skies could see 60 to 100 meteors per hour, including bright fireballs. However, some “shooting stars” will also be seen before midnight.
When And Where To Watch The Partial Solar Eclipse: North America
Although North America misses totality, millions of people will still see the moon take a noticeable bite out of the sun. The farther northeast in the U.S., the deeper the eclipse. Alaska also gets an excellent view, while eastern Canada enjoys the deepest partial eclipse anywhere on the continent.
When And Where To Watch The Partial Solar Eclipse: U.S.
Across the contiguous U.S., the partial solar eclipse begins at 10:27 a.m. MDT in Montana and North Dakota. It ends at 2:52 p.m. EDT in Maine, with the deepest eclipse visible across northern New England. Only a handful of U.S. cities will experience a partial eclipse of about 10% or greater, enough to make the event obvious through eclipse glasses. Here are some of those cities, including how much of the sun will be eclipsed at the peak of the event (and the time of the peak):
- Fairbanks, Alaska — 37% (8:27 a.m. AKDT)
- Anchorage, Alaska — 28% (8:18 a.m. AKDT)
- Presque Isle, Maine — 28% (1:50 p.m. EDT)
- Bangor, Maine — 23% (1:53 p.m. EDT)
- Portland, Maine — 19% (1:53 p.m. EDT)
- Augusta, Maine — 18% (1:52 p.m. EDT)
- Montpelier, Vermont — 17% (1:49 p.m. EDT)
- Manchester, New Hampshire — 16% (1:53 p.m. EDT)
- Boston, Massachusetts — 16% (1:55 p.m. EDT)
- Providence, Rhode Island — 15% (1:55 p.m. EDT)
- Albany, New York — 13% (1:47 p.m. EDT)
- New Haven, Connecticut — 12% (1:54 p.m. EDT)
- New York City — about 10% (1:54 p.m. EDT)
When And Where To Watch The Partial Solar Eclipse: Canada
Every Canadian province and territory will see at least part of the Aug. 12 partial solar eclipse. The event begins in western Canada shortly after 8:30 a.m. local time and continues into the late afternoon in Atlantic Canada, ending in Newfoundland and Labrador at 4:38 p.m. NDT. The deepest views will be in Nunavut and eastern Canada. Here are some notable places in Canada that will see the eclipse, including how much of the sun will be eclipsed at the peak of the event (and the time of the peak):
- Iqaluit, Nunavut — 61% (1:24 p.m. EDT)
- St. John’s, Newfoundland and Labrador — 53% (3:34 p.m. NDT)
- Moncton, New Brunswick — 32% (2:55 p.m. ADT)
- Halifax, Nova Scotia — 31% (3:00 p.m. ADT)
- Churchill, Manitoba — 27% (12:02 p.m. CDT)
- Québec City — 24% (1:46 p.m. EDT)
- Whitehorse, Yukon — 23% (9:26 a.m. MST)
- Montréal — 18% (1:45 p.m. EDT)
- Ottawa — 15% (1:42 p.m. EDT)
When To Watch The Perseids In The U.S. And Canada
The second event begins after dark. The Perseids peak overnight on Aug. 12–13 beneath one of the darkest skies in years. Under clear, rural skies, observers could see 60 to 100 meteors per hour, with activity building after midnight and peaking about 2:00 a.m. local time (i.e., the middle of the night). The meteors are tiny fragments shed by Comet 109P/Swift-Tuttle that burn up in Earth’s atmosphere at about 37 miles (59 kilometers) per second. Although they appear to radiate from the constellation Perseus, they can streak across any part of the sky. For the best experience, head somewhere away from city lights, allow your eyes 20 to 30 minutes to adapt naturally to the darkness and look up. No telescope or binoculars are required.
When And Where Is The Total Solar Eclipse?
The Aug. 12 solar eclipse is total only from a narrow path across eastern Greenland, western Iceland and northern Spain, where the moon completely covers the sun for up to 2 minutes 18 seconds. Millions more across Europe will see a deep partial eclipse, with about 91% of the sun covered in London, 92% in Paris, 85% in Berlin and 87% in Vienna. North America lies outside the path of totality, but the moon’s outer shadow still sweeps across much of Canada, Alaska and the northeastern U.S., producing a partial eclipse.
When Is The Next Total Solar Eclipse In The U.S?
The next total solar eclipse visible from the U.S. will occur on March 30, 2033, when totality crosses northern Alaska, including Nome, where the eclipsed sun will hang low above the horizon, and totality will last about two and a half minutes. The next total eclipse to reach the contiguous U.S. comes on Aug. 23, 2044, crossing parts of Montana, North Dakota and South Dakota before continuing into Canada. Just under a year later, on Aug. 12, 2045, a much broader eclipse will sweep from California to Florida, bringing up to about six minutes of totality across the central U.S.

MONTREAL – Skywatchers in Quebec and beyond will get a unique show this week, as the Perseid meteor shower coincides with a partial solar eclipse.
The Astrolab astronomy centre at the Mont-Mégantic, Que., provincial park says shooting stars will rain down from the sky between Tuesday and Friday.
On Wednesday, the meteor shower will combine with a partial solar eclipse to create a rare celestial alignment.
Sébastien Giguère, the Astrolab’s scientific coordinator, says the Perseid meteor shower can feature up to 100 shooting stars per hour, compared to about five on an average night.
“From time to time, Earth passes through a trail of dust left behind by a comet, leaving behind more dust in the solar system,” Giguère said in a phone interview. “And when Earth crosses that cloud of cosmic dust — that river of cosmic dust — well, there are more shooting stars than usual.”
The Perseids are debris from comet Swift-Tuttle, an icy ball that orbits the sun every 133 years and isn’t scheduled for a return visit until 2125.
Giguère said that while parts of Europe will experience a total solar eclipse, Canadians will witness the phenomenon partially. People in Atlantic Canada will see the highest amount of sun coverage, followed by those in eastern Quebec.
Giguère says the Astrolab, which is part of a dark sky reserve, will have activities “day and night” for people who want to witness the meteor shower, with the peak expected Wednesday.
He said people can also maximize their chances of seeing shooting stars by heading to an open area with as little light pollution as possible on a clear night and looking up.
He also wants to remind people watching the solar eclipse to use eye protection.
The organization that runs Quebec’s provincial parks says viewing conditions could be better than usual due to a new moon that doesn’t cast any light.
The Société des établissements de plein air du Québec says a partial lunar eclipse will also be visible across Quebec on the night of Aug. 27-28, providing a third astronomical event in one month.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Aug. 11, 2026.

sources.text:
Southern Californians willing to stay up late or rise before dawn will have an opportunity to view the annual Perseid meteor shower Wednesday night and early Thursday under what astronomers say should be
ideal viewing conditions.
The Perseids are expected to peak overnight, with as many as 50 to 100 meteors per hour potentially visible under dark skies, according to NASA.
Stream Los Angeles News for free, 24/7, wherever you are.
The American Meteor Society estimates observers in rural areas could see about 30 to 50 meteors per hour.
Viewing conditions are expected to be especially favorable because the meteor shower coincides with a new moon, meaning moonlight will not interfere with visibility.
The Perseids occur each year as Earth passes through debris left behind by Comet 109P/Swift-Tuttle. Tiny particles from the comet burn up as they enter Earth's atmosphere, creating the bright streaks of light commonly known as shooting stars.
The meteor shower has been observed for more than 2,000 years and is considered one of the year's most reliable and popular celestial events because of its frequent bright fireballs and its arrival during the warm summer months.
Astronomers recommend viewing the shower from a location away from city lights with an unobstructed view of the sky. The best viewing is expected between midnight and dawn, when the constellation Perseus is high in the northeastern sky. Meteors, however, may appear anywhere overhead.
Residents seeking darker skies can head to higher elevations in the San Gabriel Mountains, including Mount Wilson Observatory, Chilao Campground and Crystal Lake Recreation Area, or travel farther to Joshua Tree National Park or Red Rock Canyon State Park. Beach locations such as Leo Carrillo State Park in Malibu may also offer good viewing away from city lights.
Skywatchers are encouraged to allow about 30 minutes for their eyes to adjust to the darkness and to avoid looking at phones or other bright screens while observing.

sources.news_title: You can see both a partial solar eclipse and the Perseid meteor shower peak on the same day this week. Here’s when to look up
When and where can you see the eclipse and meteor shower in Norway?
sources.text:
Norway will soon see two major astrological events take place on the same day.
Firstly will be the (partial, in Norway) solar eclipse and then, later the same evening, the Perseid meteor shower.
The solar eclipse will be the largest in Norway for over a decade, with between 85-90 percent estimated coverage across the whole country.
In other parts of Europe, notably Spain, coverage will be 100 percent for a 'total' solar eclipse - the first in a century.
The Perseid meteor shower will reach its peak that same evening, and conditions will be particularly good because the solar eclipse means there will be a new moon and therefore little moonlight, experts say, meaning that the skies should be clear.
When can you see the eclipse and meteor shower in Norway?
On Wednesday 12th August.
According to Norwegian media, the solar eclipse will be at around 6.40 pm, depending on where in the country you are.
Then later that evening - experts say in the early morning hours from midnight on the 12th-13th — the meteor shower will appear in the sky.
Where's the best place to view them?
The first people in Norway above to view the eclipse will be in the Svalbard area, where it will take place at 18.29 p.m.
The rest of the country will catch its first glimpses of the eclipse at the following approximate times:
- Nordkapp: 18.42
- Tromsø: 18.45
- Bodø: 18.49
- Trondheim: 18.56
- Bergen: 19.02
- Oslo: 19.03
- Kristiansand: 19.06
The Perseid meteor shower will be most visible south of Dovrefjell, experts say.
How can we view them?
Experts recommend specialist solar eclipse glasses to view the eclipse safely, whilst the meteor shower should be observed from a dark location far away from artificial light.

sources.news_title: The stunning 100-strong Perseid meteor shower twinning with the solar eclipse
sources.text:
The stunning fireball Perseid meteor shower twinning with the solar eclipse
As many as 50 to 100 meteors per hour may be visible under ideal conditions
The Perseid summer light show spectacular is back – and it could be better than ever.
The stunning meteor shower will peak on Wednesday night into Thursday morning and coincides with a total solar eclipse for parts of Europe — though the best time to view the fireballs will come after totality.
As many as 50 to 100 meteors per hour may be visible under ideal conditions, according to NASA. The American Meteor Society estimates 30 to 50 meteors per hour could be seen from rural regions.
Random meteors are visible in dark skies on any given night. Meteor showers tend to put on dazzling celestial shows and happen at predictable times every year when the Earth plows through trails of debris left behind by comets and, sometimes, asteroids. Those remnants collide with Earth's atmosphere at extremely high speeds, producing streaks of light known as shooting stars.
The Perseids are debris from comet 109P/Swift-Tuttle, an icy ball that orbits the sun every 133 years and isn't scheduled for a return visit until 2125. Observations of this meteor shower date back over 2,000 years.
The Perseids are a perennial favorite because they tend to produce brilliant fireballs. Summer temperatures also make this shower popular.
"We don't have to suffer through a cold winter night to get a good view of meteors," said astronomer Zach Vanderbosch with McDonald Observatory in Texas.
The moon will be in its new moon phase during the Perseids' peak, making viewing conditions even better.
"The moon is beautiful, but it's such a diva," said astronomer Aparna Venkatesan with the University of San Francisco. "New moon means we don't have moonlight flooding the sky, and you tend to see way more meteors as a result."
How to see the Perseid meteor shower
To spot the meteors, go outside after dark, away from clouds and city lights.
The best views will be between midnight and dawn when the constellation Perseus is high in the northern sky. The meteors will appear to radiate from that constellation.
Look up and give your eyes a half hour to adjust to the darkness. Vanderbosch recommends picking a patch of sky to focus on until a quick, bright streak passes by — even in your peripheral vision — and to avoid looking at your phone.
"There's just something magical about it," Vanderbosch said.
Where can I see the solar eclipse in the UK and Ireland?
Although exact timings of the 12 August solar eclipse will vary and weather conditions may cloud visibility, in general you’ll be able to see more coverage the further south-west you are, said Royal Museums Greenwich.
First contact should be visible from 6.08pm in Scotland through to 6.18pm in Truro, Cornwall. From 7.05pm to 7.15pm destinations in the UK will see the eclipse reach its maximum, and by 8.10pm the moon will no longer be covering the sun in all areas.
For those who are planning to view the solar spectacle, eclipse glasses are crucial.

sources.news_title: The Perseid meteor shower reaches its peak this week
sources.text:
The Perseid meteor shower reaches its peak this week
On the night leading into Thursday, observers in the Northern Hemisphere will be able to watch the peak of the Perseid meteor shower: in the best conditions, 50 to 100 meteors may be seen per hour. On the same evening, Estonia will also witness a partial solar eclipse.
This year, August nights offer an exceptional spectacle: a rare parade of six planets, a solar eclipse, and the Perseid meteor shower all occur around the same time. The fireworks of warm summer nights reach their peak on Wednesday night into Thursday. According to NASA, ideal conditions can produce 50–100 meteors per hour.
In Estonia, expectations should be more modest due to geographical factors. On one hand, the radiant — the point in the sky from which meteors appear to originate — stays relatively high. On the other hand, Estonia still does not get fully dark at night, and astronomical twilight lasts all night. This means the Estonian sky will mostly reveal only the brighter flashes and larger fireballs, known as bolides.
Away from light pollution
Astronomically speaking, so‑called falling stars are actually cosmic debris. Each year, Earth passes through regions of its orbit where comets or asteroids have left behind large clouds of dust. These tiny particles rush into Earth's atmosphere at tremendous speed, begin to vaporize due to extreme temperatures, and create the familiar streaks of light seen by observers.
The Perseids originate from comet 109P/Swift‑Tuttle — a massive icy dust ball that orbits the Sun every 133 years. It will next pass near Earth in 2125. Humanity has admired this comet's dust trail in the sky for more than 2,000 years.
The Perseids are considered the most anticipated meteor shower of the year for several reasons. First, they are known for very bright fireballs. Second, warm summer weather makes observing comfortable, unlike winter meteor showers. This year, conditions are especially favorable because the peak coincides with a new moon, meaning meteors do not have to compete with moonlight.
For the best viewing experience, head outdoors after darkness falls. Light pollution brightens the sky and hides weaker flashes. Scientists recommend finding a clear, dark location far from city lights.
The densest meteor activity will be visible from midnight to dawn on the night leading into Thursday. Human eyes need time to adjust to darkness: astronomers advise giving your eyes at least half an hour and avoiding all light sources. Even a quick glance at a bright screen resets your night vision instantly.
For targeted viewing, lie on your back. Astronomer Zach Vanderbosch of the McDonald Observatory in Texas suggests choosing one area of the sky and keeping your gaze fixed there. After adjusting to the dark, the eye will catch even quick flashes out of the corner of your vision.
A good year for skywatching
In Estonia, August nights are already long and dark enough for skywatching. The northern location offers an advantage, as the constellation Perseus — which gives the Perseids their name — rises above the horizon relatively early. Local amateur astronomers recommend dressing warmly for the night: a sleeping mat or blankets help protect against ground moisture and cold.
When watching falling stars, it is worth remembering that the dust particles causing them are usually the size of a tiny grain of sand. Despite their small mass, enormous kinetic energy is released when they enter the atmosphere. Larger particles, about the size of a pea, can leave a glowing smoke trail in the sky for several seconds.
Annual observations give scientists important information: the density and distribution of particles in the meteor stream help refine models of comet fragmentation. Dust trails are not evenly distributed in space, and denser clouds along the orbit provide valuable insight into the movement of cosmic material.
As mentioned, Estonia will also see a partial solar eclipse on 12 August. In Tallinn, the astronomical event begins at 20:02. The partial eclipse reaches its maximum at 20:53, when the Sun resembles a thin crescent. The entire event lasts one hour and 18 minutes, ending at 21:19 as the Sun dips below the horizon.
--
Editor: Airika Harrik, Argo Ideon

sources.text:
PODCAST:
August 10, 2026 ~ Michael Narlock, the Cranbrook Institute’s Head of Astronomy discusses this week’s Perseid meteor shower and eclipse.
BLOOMFIELD HILLS ~ A partial solar eclipse will be visible across the country midday Wednesday, followed by a Perseid meteor shower on Wednesday night. The Perseid meteor shower is an annual display of “shooting stars” caused by bits of comet dust burning up in Earth’s atmosphere. Cranbrook Institute of Science is inviting the community to view both astronomical events.
Cranbrook Institute astronomy head Mike Narlock told Focus with Paul W. Smith guest host Dave LewAllen the mid-week forecast could offer ideal viewing conditions. “If the heavens open up, then on the evening of Wednesday, August 12 into the morning of August 13, we’ll be experiencing the peak of the Perseid meteor shower.”
SOCIAL MEDIA:
The partial eclipse marks the moon’s passing between the sun and Earth, briefly obscuring a small portion of the sun. Totality, full coverage of the sun, will not occur anywhere in the United States. In Michigan, NASA predicts about 3% coverage at roughly 1:30 p.m.
The Perseids have been active since mid-July, but their activity will peak Wednesday night as Earth moves through the densest part of the comet’s debris trail. The annual mid-summer shower aligns with a new moon this year, reducing moonlight and improving visibility. NASA said dark skies could reveal up to 100 meteors per hour in rural areas.
If conditions are clear, Wednesday will offer a rare pairing of astronomical events: a muted dip in sunlight followed by a surge of meteors streaking overhead. For Michigan observers, it’s a chance to watch two celestial events unfold within the span of a single day. Cranbrook will host eclipse viewing opportunities in the afternoon and a Perseid meteor shower program Wednesday evening. Tickets and details are available at Science.Cranbrook.edu.

sources.news_title: Perseid Meteor Shower Peaks August 12: Up to 100 Shooting Stars Per Hour Expected
sources.text:
The annual Perseid meteor shower reaches its magnificent peak on the night of August 12 into the early hours of August 13, producing up to 100 shooting stars per hour under ideal night skies. Renowned as the most popular celestial event of the summer, this year’s display offers an extraordinary astronomical alignment, coinciding directly with the rare August 12 total solar eclipse across Greenland, Iceland, and Spain.
Because the peak arrives during the New Moon phase, the sky will be completely dark with zero moonlight interference all night long. Observers across Europe, North America, and worldwide will enjoy prime viewing conditions from dusk until the pre-dawn hours as the constellation Perseus climbs higher into the northeastern sky.
No matter where you live on Earth, two great meteor showers happen yearly: the summer Perseids in August and the Geminids in December. Both events are famously reliable, consistently producing a zenithal hourly rate (ZHR)* exceeding 100 meteors under dark, pristine skies.
These days, the Perseid meteor shower is already ramping up, with an increasing number of meteors every night. The peak intensity will happen from August 11th to 13th this year.
*ZHR – The Zenithal Hourly Rate of any meteor shower tells us the number of meteors a single observer would see in an hour of peak activity if it were at the zenith. The conditions are considered excellent (stars are visible up to magnitude 6.5). The rate that can effectively be seen is nearly always lower and decreases the closer the radiant is to the horizon.

What is the Perseid meteor shower?
The Perseid meteors are small dust particles, crumbs of comet 109P/Swift-Tuttle, burning up as they hit our atmosphere at about 59 km/s. They are known as one of the most regular and reliable meteor showers, peaking in mid-August of every year. They are so dependable that they used to be known as tears of St. Lawrence for decades.
The Perseid meteor shower is rich in bright, colorful meteors, including fireballs. The celestial show occurs high in the atmosphere, well above the regular weather, at altitudes of about 100 km—right at the edge of space.
While they may seem close, the Perseids appearing overhead will be about 100 km away, while those close to the horizon will be 500 km away or more.
An average bright Perseid meteor is produced by a dust particle (called a meteoroid) that is only several millimeters across. The brightest Perseids often leave persistent dust trails, slowly twisted and contorted by the upper-level winds.
They can last tens of seconds if you watch them with the naked eye and minutes if you use binoculars.
Finding the spot where the Perseids come out in the sky is pretty simple. All the meteors will look like they come from a point in the constellation of Perseus. If you trace all the Perseid meteors backward, they all seem to come from the constellation Perseus, near the famous Double Cluster. Hence, the meteor shower is named in honor of the constellation Perseus, the Hero.
This point in the sky is called the radiant. The higher the radiant is in the sky, the more meteors appear.

The best opportunities to see the Perseids will begin right after sunset on August 12 and continue throughout the night until dawn.
To observe or photograph the Perseid meteor shower, find a spot with the clearest skies possible, far from city lights. Heading to elevated locations in hills or mountains will provide darker skies and clearer atmospheric clarity for capturing fireballs.

What equipment do we need?
We need a camera, lens, tripod, and some luck. However, when it comes to meteor photography, more specific equipment is necessary to get the best results out of your photography attempts.
- A digital camera with the option of making long exposures. Any interchangeable lens camera (DSLR or mirrorless) will have this option, including compact cameras, and some phone cameras nowadays can also take long exposures
- A tripod. The stronger, the better. Especially if you plan to photograph in higher elevations, where winds could be stronger
- A remote trigger for the camera (or timer) that helps you to photograph continuously and without shaking the camera when pressing the shutter button
- And indeed… a meteor shower. Preferably the highest activity possible, so during the peak nights

What to expect?
What can you expect as you are ready to enter the field?
First, be ready to take many photos before you catch a meteor. Be prepared to spend at least an hour or two under the starry sky to catch a good one, even in the strongest of meteor showers, like the summer’s Perseid meteor shower or the Geminids in winter.
Photographing a Perseid meteor shower can often bring hours and hours of taking hundreds or even thousands of photos. But, when things go right… whoa! Imagine you catch an exploding fireball. You will forget all the waiting until then!
Conclusion – Perseid meteor shower 2026: A spectacular display with no Moon
What can we say at the end? The Perseid meteor shower is one of those celestial events you don’t want to miss. Seriously! Moonless nights are spectacular!
The main downside of the summer months is the weather disturbance from the daytime thunderstorm activity; the remaining clouds often extend into the nighttime hours. But weather patterns are changing, so we might get lucky and see stable weather with low cloud coverage and thunderstorm activity around the peak.
The Perseid meteor shower this year is expected to produce around 90-120 meteors per hour during both nights around the peak, on August 11th and 12th. The Perseids’ main peak occurs around August 13th, 2 UTC.
This is almost as perfect as it gets for Europe, but it is a bit less favorable for the United States and Canada since the peak occurs around 6 hours before midnight.
To conclude, it is advised to go out, observe, and photograph the Perseids from dusk all the way until dawn, as the absence of moonlight provides ideal, pitch-black viewing conditions all night long. We only need clear skies!
